name: Matryoshka, Quantised and Reduced Embeddings
question: Can the vectors be smaller without losing recall?
summary: Shrink vectors to save memory, storage and search time. Matryoshka-trained models let you simply keep the first dimensions. Quantization stores each value in fewer bits. PCA projects onto the directions that matter most. Recall usually drops a little, so measure it.
useCases: Large corpora where the index no longer fits in memory
Latency budgets that full-size vectors can’t meet
Edge or mobile search with tight storage

steps.title: Record the baseline
steps.text: Measure recall@10 and memory at full size first: 1,536 float32 dimensions take 6,144 bytes per vector.

steps.title: Truncate a Matryoshka model
steps.text: Models trained Matryoshka-style put the most information in the first dimensions, so asking for 512 keeps about 99% of recall at a third of the size.

steps.title: Quantize to int8
steps.text: Store each value in 8 bits instead of 32 with a per-dimension scale: 512 bytes per vector, 4× smaller again, with a small recall loss.

steps.title: Or go binary
steps.text: Keep only the sign of each dimension: 1 bit each, 192 bytes for 1,536 dimensions, 32× smaller. On its own, recall falls to about 0.82.

steps.title: Oversample, then rescore
steps.text: Fetch 4× more candidates by fast Hamming distance, then rescore them with the full-precision vectors. Most of the lost recall comes back.

steps.title: Choose by measured recall
steps.text: Pick the smallest setting whose recall you can accept. Here 512-dimension int8 keeps 98% of recall at 12× less memory.

library.name: OpenAI embeddings + NumPy
library.what: text-embedding-3 models accept a dimensions parameter (Matryoshka truncation); NumPy handles int8 and binary quantization.

samples.code:
import numpy as np
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()

resp = client.embeddings.create(model="text-embedding-3-large",
                                input=["Auto-debit for SIP instalments"],
                                dimensions=512)             # Matryoshka truncation
v = np.array(resp.data[0].embedding, dtype=np.float32)     # 512 × 4 B

scale = np.abs(v).max() / 127
v_int8 = np.round(v / scale).astype(np.int8)               # 4× smaller
v_bin = np.packbits(v > 0)                                 # 32× smaller

print(v.nbytes, v_int8.nbytes, v_bin.nbytes)               # 2048 512 64

numericDrill.question: 10 million vectors at 1,024 float32 dimensions. How much memory with int8 quantization, in GB?

interview.question: What is Matryoshka representation learning?
interview.answer: Training an embedding model so the first dimensions carry the most information, like nested dolls. You can truncate vectors (say 1,536 → 256) and keep most of the quality without retraining.

interview.question: Scalar or binary quantization?
interview.answer: Scalar (int8) stores each value in 8 bits: 4× smaller with a small recall loss. Binary stores 1 bit per dimension: 32× smaller but a larger loss, usually recovered by oversampling and re-ranking with full vectors.

mistakes.mistake: Truncating vectors from a model not trained for it

mistakes.fix: Measure retrieval metrics in the full space

quiz.question: 30 million vectors × 1,024 float32 dimensions. How much memory do the raw vectors need?
The same 30 million × 1,024 vectors are quantized to int8. How much memory now?
quiz.explanation: 1,024 B × 30 million ≈ 30.7 GB, 4× smaller.

quiz.question: 100 million vectors of 1,024 dimensions are binary quantized. How much memory?
quiz.explanation: 1,024 bits = 128 B × 100 million = 12.8 GB.

quiz.question: Which statements about Matryoshka embeddings are true? Select all that apply.
options: The model is trained so the first dimensions carry the most information
Truncating a model not trained this way loses much more quality
Vectors should be re-normalized after truncation before cosine search
Each truncation size needs a retrained model
quiz.explanation: One Matryoshka model supports many sizes; you just keep the first dimensions and re-normalize.

quiz.question: Binary quantization cut memory 32×, but recall dropped. What is the standard remedy?
options: Oversample candidates and rescore them with full-precision vectors
quiz.explanation: Fetch more cheap candidates, then re-sort them precisely: most recall comes back.

quiz.question: A UMAP plot of note embeddings shows two diagnoses overlapping. What should you conclude?
options: Nothing firm: 2-D projections distort distances, so measure retrieval directly
Search will fail for both diagnoses
quiz.explanation: UMAP and t-SNE are for inspection, not proof. Check recall on real queries.

quiz.question: 1,536 float32 dimensions are reduced to 256 dimensions in int8. How much smaller is each vector?
You use OpenAI text-embedding-3-small and want 512-dimension vectors without training anything. How?
options: Pass dimensions=512 in the embeddings request
Run PCA on each single vector
quiz.explanation: text-embedding-3 models support a dimensions parameter because they were trained Matryoshka-style.

quiz.question: Which statements about product quantization are true? Select all that apply.
options: It splits each vector into sub-vectors
It stores a codebook ID for each sub-vector
Its codebooks are learned from the data
quiz.explanation: PQ compresses heavily by approximating sub-vectors with learned centroids, so some accuracy is lost.

quiz.question: Your embedding model was not trained Matryoshka-style, and you need 256 dimensions. What is the better option?
options: Fit PCA on a sample and project, then measure recall, or switch to a Matryoshka model
Keep the first 256 values and assume nothing changes
Round values to one decimal place
quiz.explanation: Naive truncation discards information spread across all dimensions in such a model.

quiz.question: You need the top 10 results and oversample 4× before rescoring. How many candidates are rescored?
quiz.explanation: 10 × 4 = 40 candidates.

quiz.question: A newsroom index holds 200,000 vectors at 768 float32 dimensions on a 16 GB server. Should you compress?
options: Probably not: about 614 MB already fits comfortably
quiz.explanation: 768 × 4 B = 3,072 B × 200,000 ≈ 614 MB. Compression would cost recall for no gain.

quiz.question: What should you measure before and after compressing an index? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Compression trades recall for memory and speed. Measure all three.

quiz.question: How many bytes does a 1,536-dimension float16 vector take?
quiz.explanation: 1,536 × 2 B = 3,072 B, half of float32.

quiz.question: In a binary index with rescoring, where do the full-precision vectors usually live?
options: On disk or cheaper storage, read only for the candidates
In RAM next to the binary vectors, always
quiz.explanation: RAM holds the compact index; the full vectors are fetched only to rescore a few candidates.

quiz.question: Which practices make int8 quantization safer? Select all that apply.
options: Calibrate value ranges on a representative sample
Keep the float32 originals for rescoring
Compute the scale from a single vector
quiz.explanation: A range taken from one vector clips values in others. Calibrate, measure and keep originals.

quiz.question: Which of these reduce the memory an index needs? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: More overlap creates more chunks, which increases memory.

quiz.question: A team truncated a 1,024-dimension model that was not trained Matryoshka-style to 128 dimensions, and recall collapsed. Why?
options: Its information is spread across all dimensions, so the first 128 lose most of it
128 is below the minimum any database accepts
Cosine similarity needs at least 256 dimensions
quiz.explanation: Only Matryoshka-trained models concentrate information in the first dimensions.

quiz.question: What is the Hamming distance between binary codes 1011 and 1101?
quiz.explanation: They differ in the second and third positions: distance 2.

quiz.question: You want binary quantization with oversampling and rescoring configured per collection, without custom code. Which tool fits?
quiz.explanation: Qdrant supports scalar, binary and product quantization with rescoring settings.
